title: Italy putting nearly all major cities on highest heat alert
description: In its latest heatwave bulletin published on Saturday, the Italian health ministry says that by Monday, some 25 of the country's 27 major cities will
body: In its latest heatwave bulletin published on Saturday, the Italian health ministry says that by Monday, some 25 of the country's 27 major cities will be on red alert.It says it expects only  two - Reggio Calabria in the southern tip of Italy's "boot" and Messina, facing it across on the island of Sicily - to be on the second-highest "amber" alert.The ministry urges residents in the affected areas to avoid exposure to heat and direct sunlight during the hottest hours between 11:00 and 18:00, stay indoors and drink plenty of fluids.The extreme heat is being caused by a subtropical anticyclone from North Africa that is now strengthening over the Mediterranean.Meanwhile, firefighters in Greece, France, Portugal and Spain are still tackling blazes spanning thousands of hectares.In France, some 2,500 people were evacuated in the south-eastern Var region on Friday evening after a blaze - which had been contained for several days - reignited, local officials said.But a massive fire in the south-western Gironde region is now under control, and some 200,000 local evacuated residents have been able to return to their homes.

schema.headline: Italy putting nearly all major cities on highest heat alert

title: British-Nepali climber Nirmal Purja killed in Pakistan avalanche, his company says
description: Renowned British-Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja is among 10 people killed in an avalanche on Broad Peak in Pakistan, his company has said.Elite Exped
body: Renowned British-Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja is among 10 people killed in an avalanche on Broad Peak in Pakistan, his company has said.Elite Expeditions said it confirmed with "profound sadness and immense heartbreak" that Purja, 43, had died in Thursday's avalanche. His brother Kamal later wrote: "We will miss you every single day".Purja, who was born in Nepal and later served in the British army, was known for scaling the world's 14 highest peaks in just over six months in 2019.Pakistani officials earlier said the bodies of three climbers from his expedition - American Mallory Geis, Nadhira Ahmed Abdullah Al Harthy from Oman and Pur Bahadur Gurung from Nepal - had been recovered.Purja's death was also confirmed by Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah, who said that "the tragic death of six Nepalese and four other foreign climbers, including world record holder Nirmal Purja, in the Karakoram mountain range of Pakistan, has shocked us"."The history of their courage, dedication, and contributions will always remain inspiring," the prime minister added.In a statement, Purja's older brother Kamal wrote: "It is with the heaviest heart that I share the devastating news that my beloved younger brother, Nirmal 'Nimsdai' Purja, and the other climbers are no longer with us."Although our hearts are broken, we are incredibly proud of you. Your legacy will live forever," he added.UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said in a post on X: "Incredibly sad to learn of the passing of Nirmal (Nims) Purja and those he was climbing with."He was an inspirational man who served in our Armed Forces for many years - and whose incredible mountaineering adventures are known the world over."Naila Kiani, a spokesperson for the Alpine Club of Pakistan which is involved in the rescue efforts, told BBC's Newshour programme that Purja had led many expeditions that she was on. Praising his leadership skills, she described him as a "very experienced climber and fearless".Kiani said the Alpine Club would only announce his death once the body has been recovered - but she added that "we are fearing them all dead".She also said rescuers had seen some bodies - but were yet to reach them.Teams in Pakistan have been searching for the climbers on the world's 12th-highest summit after an avalanche on the 8,047m (26,400ft) peak in the Karakoram range.The multinational climbing group was being led by Purja. Also known as Nims, he rose to prominence in 2019 when he climbed all 14 of the world's mountains with peaks above 8,000m in 189 days - smashing the previous record by more than seven years.He became widely known following a Netflix documentary chronicling his journey, 14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible, released two years later.At the time, he said: "It has been a gruelling but humbling six months, and I hope to have proven that anything is possible with some determination, self-belief and positivity."Purja served in the British military for 16 years, 10 of which were spent in the special forces, and he was awarded an MBE by the late Queen in 2018 for his achievement in extreme high-altitude mountaineering.Purja, who lived with his wife and three-year-old daughter in Hampshire in southern England, said he was also the first Gurkha to climb Everest while serving in the British military.In his last post on X, published on Monday, he said he had not intended to climb Broad Peak."Initially, the plan was to climb just G2," Purja wrote, referring to Gasherbrum II, another peak in the Karakoram mountain range.But right before he set off for Pakistan, he realised that if he also managed to climb Broad Peak while he was there, he would have only one more mountain to conquer before becoming the "first person in history to climb all 14 eight-thousanders twice. Without oxygen."An eight-thousander is a mountain that rises more than 8,000m above sea level."This wasn't planned," Purja wrote. "But opportunities don't scream: they whisper to those already working in silence.""Broad Peak, I ask for nothing but safe passage up and back down. I take zero mountains for granted," he wrote.Broad Peak is regarded as one of the more challenging mountains for climbers. The first successful ascent was in 1957, when an Austrian expedition reached the summit.Since then, many more have climbed the mountain, but dozens have lost their lives.One of Broad Peak's deadliest years was 2013, when at least six fatalities were recorded.

title: Danube's record low levels force shutdown of Hungary's only nuclear plant
description: Image source, EPAImage caption, The level of the water of the Danube is so low that the nuclear power plant's suction nozzles cannot reach itByLaura G
body: Image source, EPAImage caption, The level of the water of the Danube is so low that the nuclear power plant's suction nozzles cannot reach itByLaura Gozzi and Paul KirbyEurope digital editorHungary's only nuclear power plant will be forced to shut down entirely for the first time due to record low water levels of the River Danube, Prime Minister Péter Magyar has said.The Soviet-era Paks power plant uses the Danube for cooling but the water level is so low that the suction nozzles cannot reach it. Magyar warned Hungary's energy supply could become "critical" from Monday due to the Paks shutdown and the ongoing heatwave, which will see temperatures hover around 37C for a week.Like much of Europe, Hungary has seen very low rainfall and high temperatures for much of the summer.The waters of the Danube have fallen to the lowest levels for 30 years in several countries, including neighbouring Serbia and Romania.Magyar asked Hungarians to limit activities that required significant energy consumption between the peak times of 17:00 and 22:00, including charging electric cars and using air conditioning equipment.A "rotational shutdown regime" was also possible if the other combined efforts were not enough to maintain the balance of the national grid, Magyar said, adding the government would compile a list of electricity and water consumers whose consumption could be limited.Image source, Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, Large areas of the riverbed have been exposed in the centre of Budapest after weeks of extreme heat and droughtIn Romania, one of the country's only two nuclear reactors has been shut down at the Cernavoda power plant, which provides about 20% of the country's power.The first of the two 706-megawatt reactors was shut down earlier this week because the Danube's levels were so low, and state-owned company Nuclearelectrica was trying to avoid closing down the other on Thursday. If the second reactor is shut down Romania will, like Hungary, be temporarily without any nuclear energy production.Climate change is driving up temperatures around the world - but particularly in Europe.It is the fasting warming continent, heating up twice as fast as the global average, according to the Copernicus climate service. This is causing increased summer heatwaves, greater pressure on Europe's waters and more intense wildfires. Image source, ReutersImage caption, Among the wrecks exposed by the low levels of the Danube was a World War Two German warship at Prahovo in SerbiaRomania's National Institute of Hydrology says the average river flow where the Danube enters the country is 4,700 cubic metres per second in July, whereas on Wednesday it was down to less than a third of that, at 1,600cm per second. The institute forecast it would continue to fall to 1,500cm per second by Tuesday.The Danube runs 2,857km (1,775 miles) through 19 countries.The Upper Danube goes from Germany to the Slovak capital Bratislava, the middle basin runs from Bratislava to the border between Serbia and Romania and the Lower Danube extends through Romania and Bulgaria into the three main branches of the Danube Delta that flow into the Black Sea.The low waters of the river have resulted in several unexpected discoveries. The remains of a sunken Hungarian cargo ship resurfaced in Croatia, while the hulks of a German river flotilla was seen in Serbia. And a resident of the northeastern Bulgarian city of Ruse found bones on the Danube river bed, which experts determined were the remains of a mammoth. They were able to recognise a lower jaw, two tusks, and possibly a mammoth rib.Image source, Inquam Photos/Ovidiu Micsik/ReutersImage caption, River flow in Serbia on the Danube is now a third of the average for JulyShipping has ground to a halt on the river in Bulgaria, and border police had to evacuate 186 river cruise passengers from the Viking Ullur ship earlier this week when it ran aground close to Vidin, a city that sits on the border with Romania.  There were reports of passengers running low of food and water because the cruise ship was unable to dock in Vidin, but Viking later told the BBC that "sufficient water remained available for all guests and crew throughout the incident. At no point did the vessel run out of provisions or experience a shortage"."I have never heard of such low levels over the years. There has certainly not been a similar situation since 1990," Ivan Zhekov, head of river supervision at Bulgaria's maritime administration agency told BTA news agency.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Boats lie on the dried-out Danube riverbed in front of the Calafat-Vidin bridge, connecting Bulgaria and RomaniaIt is not just the Danube where river levels are low. In Serbia, the levels are also very low on the Sava and Tisa, which are both tributaries of the Danube.Serbian hydrologist Dejan Vladiković said the problems were not just down to the current high temperatures but also to low rainfall during the spring. He told Serbian TV channel N1 that the Danube was down to levels not seen for 50 to 60 years, and climatologists did not expect to see any improvement until mid-September.Temperatures in Serbia are set to climb as high as 38C on Friday, and locally up to 40C, with night-time temperatures in Belgrade as high as 26C.Elsewhere in Europe, forecasters say fire-prone conditions are expected to spread towards central Europe, with Greece and Turkey among the countries worst affected. Vast areas of France and Spain have just experienced some of the most intense and widespread wildfires in living memory, leading to hundreds of thocusands of evacuations.Correction 1 August: This article originally stated that food and water had been running low for passengers on the grounded Viking Ullur and another boat was unable to get close enough with provisions. It was later amended with the company's denial of any shortage.

schema.headline: Danube's record low levels force shutdown of Hungary's only nuclear plant

title: Peru's ex-president leaves jail after 15-year jail term for corruption overturned
description: Peru's constitutional court has overturned a 15-year jail sentence handed to the country's former president after he was found guilty of corruption.Ol
body: Peru's constitutional court has overturned a 15-year jail sentence handed to the country's former president after he was found guilty of corruption.Ollanta Humala, who led the country from 2011 to 2016, was convicted in 2025 of accepting illegal funds from the Venezuelan president and Brazilian construction company Odebrecht to fund his election campaigns in 2006 and 2011. The former president had said he would appeal against the verdict, and now Peru's constitutional court has declared the entire criminal proceedings against him null and void. Humala was released from Barbadillo Prison in the capital Lima on Friday night, with a crowd of supporters on hand to see his release.After the ruling, Humala's lawyer Julio Espinoza Goyena wrote on social media that the court had decided the contributions his client received on electoral campaigns "do not constitute money laundering".He said: "The Criminal Chamber currently handling the case must order the definitive dismissal of the proceedings and the FREEDOM of former President Ollanta Humala". When Humala was convicted, his wife Nadine Heredia was also found guilty of money laundering and sentenced to 15 years in prison. However, she was granted safe passage to Brazil after seeking asylum in the Brazilian embassy."We have been victims of political and judicial persecution," Humala told reporters outside the small prison facility.Humala was the first of four Peruvian presidents to be investigated in connection with the Odebrecht scandal. Alejandro Toledo, who governed from 2001 to 2006, was sentenced last year to more than 20 years in prison for taking $35m (£26m) in bribes from the company.Alan García, president from 1985 to 1990 and 2006 to 2011, killed himself in 2019 as he faced imminent arrest over allegations he was bribed by Odebrecht. He had denied the accusations.Pedro Pablo Kuczynski, in office from 2016 to 2018, faced impeachment proceedings after it emerged that Odebrecht had paid him millions of dollars in his previous government role.The investigation is ongoing. Kuczynski has always maintained the payments were not illegal.At their own trial, Humala and his wife, with whom he cofounded the Nationalist Party, were accused of accepting $3m in illegal contributions from the firm, which they used to finance his 2011 presidential campaign.They were also accused of taking $200,000 from Venezuelan leader Hugo Chávez to bankroll the 2006 campaign.But the couple always maintained that they were the victims of political persecution.Humala, a former army officer, came to national prominence in 2000 when he led a short-live military rebellion against then-president Alberto Fujimori.In 2006, he ran for president on a platform inspired by the socialist revolution of Venezuela's Chávez. After an unsuccessful first attempt, Humala ran again in 2011; this time on a more moderate platform emulating the policies of Brazil's then-president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva to defeat right-wing rival Keiko Fujimori, the eldest daughter of Alberto Fujimori.His legal troubles started shortly after his term finished in 2016, when Odebrecht admitted to bribing Latin American government officials and political parties with hundreds of millions of dollars to win business.Prosecutors accused Humala and his wife of receiving millions from Odebrecht, as well as the illegal funding from Chávez to finance the 2006 presidential campaign.Humala and Heredia were subsequently placed in pre-trial detention for a year, before they were eventually convicted in 2025.

schema.headline: Peru's ex-president leaves jail after 15-year jail term for corruption overturned

title: Spain attacks 'selfish' response of some EU countries to Ceuta migrant crossings
description: Spain has condemned the "selfish, polarising and unlawful" reaction of some EU countries to the influx of about 60,000 migrants from Morocco into the
body: Spain has condemned the "selfish, polarising and unlawful" reaction of some EU countries to the influx of about 60,000 migrants from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. Spanish officials say almost all those who reached Ceuta on 30 July have returned, while Spain's interior minister said on Saturday that the death toll from the surge in crossings had risen to at least 67. Italy temporarily suspended the EU's border-free Schengen arrangement with Spain, as PM Giorgia Meloni called the scenes "shocking". Finland and Denmark backed Italy's move, while Czech PM Andrej Babiš urged a temporary suspension of Spain's Schengen membership.EU interior ministers will meet on Tuesday by video conference to discuss the issue.Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez had called for an urgent meeting to "reaffirm that the security of our external borders is a shared responsibility of all Member States".Twenty-two of the EU's 27 countries also called for emergency talks in an open letter, citing "serious concerns" regarding the developments in Ceuta.The nations "welcome that Spain and Morocco are cooperating closely to ensure the swift return of migrants", but said a video conference would help reach agreement on mobilising EU instruments and support for Spain to restore "effective control" of the border and prevent further uncontrolled crossings.In a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he had "serious concerns" about some European governments.He said the Spanish government had fully restored control over the border and prevented any "unauthorised onward movement towards continental Europe" in less than 48 hours.While most had shown "support and solidarity", Sanchez said other European governments had chosen to attack Spain, "driven by prejudice, fake news, ignorance, or political interest", and pointed out that Ceuta was not part of the Schengen area. "The European Union cannot afford this kind of selfish, polarising and unlawful reaction," he said.Also on Saturday, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he had spoken to Sánchez and the UK was "providing what help we can". But while the situation on the ground appears to be easing, political and diplomatic fallout is rippling through Madrid and other capitals. On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote on social media that such "uncontrolled immigration" was a threat to national security, before suspending the Schengen zone agreement with Spain for a month.The Schengen Area is a system of open borders spanning 29 European countries that have abolished controls at their common borders.Spain responded by summoning the Italian ambassador to Madrid, while its foreign minister said he expected "European solidarity and not partisan demagoguery".Finland's Interior Minister Mari Rantanen said she had started preparations for restoring internal border checks "if the need arises". She also urged "all European countries" to support Meloni's move.Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen also urged the EU to "consider all options, including a suspension of Schengen co-operation".France has tightened checks on its border with Spain and said it would increase its police presence by Saturday.Portuguese PM Luis Montenegro said he was considering reinforcing border checks.Von der Leyen said the images from Ceuta were "unacceptable". "We cannot allow anyone to come to our Union without abiding by our rules," she said on social media.German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he "supports Spain's intention not to allow illegal migrants onto the European continent", and demanded that Morocco "take back illegal migrants immediately".In the US, the State Department said the incident was a direct result of Spain's migration policies. President Donald Trump called the situation a "catastrophe" and said "it looks like an invasion of a country by hundreds of thousands of people".Spain has defended its handling of the migrant surge. Madrid has sent troops, more police, drones, divers and boats to Ceuta. The country has also deployed its armed forces to bolster security in another Spanish enclave, Melilla, where hundreds of crossings were also reported.Sánchez, who has visited Ceuta after the migrant influx, said he would consider reinforcing the border with Morocco, and that Moroccan authorities were co-operating.He blamed trafficking gangs for the migrant surge, calling the incident a "violation of Spain's territorial integrity"."Trafficking mafias took a self-serving interpretation of a Supreme Court ruling" which "spread like wildfire", he said.EU Commissioner Magnus Brunner said, after a phone call with Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares, that "not a single person has crossed to mainland EU".In June, Spain's Supreme Court ruled that migrants stopped at sea while trying to reach Ceuta or Melilla could not be summarily returned to Morocco without due process.While the surge of migrants this year is extraordinary, Ceuta has long been a focal point for migrants attempting to reach Europe. During the summer months, there is often a big push to reach Ceuta, typically organised over social media.In 2021, about 8,000 people entered Ceuta over a matter of days, exacerbating Spain's diplomatic tensions with Morocco.

schema.headline: Spain attacks 'selfish' response of some EU countries to Ceuta migrant crossings

title: CJP protest: India's 'Cockroach' protesters have wounds consistent with pellet-gun fire, experts say
description: Independent ballistic experts have told the BBC that injuries sustained by some Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) supporters during last week's protest in t
body: Independent ballistic experts have told the BBC that injuries sustained by some Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) supporters during last week's protest in the Indian capital were caused by pellet guns.Warning: This story contains images some might find distressingCentral Delhi witnessed overwhelming violence on 20 July when tens of thousands of protesters tried to march to the parliament to seek education reforms and the resignation of the education minister.Police and paramilitary personnel were seen brutally attacking the crowds with wooden sticks, batons and tear gas. Delhi Police said 60 protesters and 118 of their personnel were injured. CJP said the number of injured protesters was a lot higher than the official count.In the days following the crackdown, the government has not confirmed media reports that pellet guns were used on protesters.But the BBC has been able to confirm at least four cases where protesters have been treated at hospitals for wounds that experts say are caused by pellet guns.Shotguns designed for bird hunting are sometimes referred to as pellet guns. They fire cartridges, known as "birdshot", containing 200 to 400 small metal pellets. When used against crowds, the pellets spread out in a wide arc, striking people indiscriminately. These guns are banned in several countries.We have spoken to two of the injured men who believe they were hit by pellet guns fired by security forces. We have also shown photographs and videos of them and a third man to two independent armament and forensic experts. A senior official at a hospital has confirmed a fourth man who also received treatment for pellet wounds.The experts say the dozens of tiny round punctures are tell-tale signs of injuries caused by birdshot."The injuries depicted are definitely from a pellet gun," UK-based ballistics forensic scientist Philip Boyce told the BBC, adding that the weapon used is "a 12-gauge pump-action shotgun". "These pellet injuries can actually be quite devastating, especially at close range. The injuries I see [in Delhi] are not at close range, they're at least 50 feet. But they can actually still be devastating and potentially life-threatening even from 100 feet," he said.NR Jenzen-Jones, director of Armament Research Services (ARES) in UK, told the BBC that "images and video from the protests show the police using shotguns for crowd control" and photos of "injuries are strongly consistent with the use of birdshot"."While shotguns are a common tool in the less-lethal arsenals of many states, Indian law enforcement agencies have a long history of employing shotgun cartridges loaded with small lead pellets - known as 'birdshot' - in crowd-control scenarios. When loaded with birdshot cartridges, shotguns are sometimes referred to as 'pellet guns'," he added."But these pellets are not safe. They can result in life-changing or, occasionally, life-threatening injuries. They also pepper the body with toxic lead, which can sometimes be difficult to remove safely," he said.That's why many countries have either banned them or restricted their usage. In the UK, Boyce says the guns are widely used for shooting birds and they're fairly freely available. But, he's "not aware" of any instance when they've been used for crowd control.In Indian-administered Kashmir - where pellet guns have been used since 2010 - official data,, external compiled by Human Rights Watch, shows they have injured several thousand people, killed at least 17 and blinded dozens. If it's confirmed that the forces used pellet guns in Delhi, this would be the first time that India would have used them on its citizens in its capital city.Two of the young men we spoke to told us they were injured in Connaught Place - a major hub near parliament - after 4pm local time on 20 July.Mohit (name changed) said when he saw a security personnel aim his gun at him, he turned around and began running in the opposite direction."Two-three seconds later, I felt a burning sensation on my right arm and back," the 28-year-old journalist told the BBC.Mohit said he kept running as a searing pain coursed through his body until he reached a café, bought a bottle of water and washed his wounds. "That's when I saw the tiny circular holes on my arm and upper back. I was completely freaked out." An X-ray taken at Safdarjung hospital, where he was treated for his wounds, shows tiny objects embedded in his arm and upper torso. Medical records that he has shared with the BBC show he has 26 pellet wounds on his right elbow and four on his upper right back. The notes include a diagram showing where the objects are lodged in his body.Mohit said the doctors told him that surgery could worsen his situation, but he worries about the damage "they can do in future since they remain lodged in my body or whether the ugly scars would ever go away"."But after seeing photos of other victims who've been hit in the face, I'm feeling fortunate," he says.Shaikh Irshad Mansoori, who works at a Gurugram-based firm, was not so fortunate.He was walking from Connaught Place to Jantar Mantar, the main CJP protest venue, when "the police and RAF [Rapid Action Force, a paramilitary force] personnel began beating the crowd with sticks and firing tear gas, causing a stampede-like situation and panic"."I was with a group of protesters and we were raising slogans when an RAF personnel pointed his gun at us. We didn't think he would fire, but then I suddenly heard a cracking sound nearby and pellets hit me on my left eyebrow and my chin."Some protesters tried to stem his bleeding with items of clothing, hailed a passing vehicle and took him to Lady Hardinge hospital.He said scans showed he had more than 40 pellets in his body, including three embedded deep in his neck, left eye muscle and under his nose that doctors told him needed to be taken out."Surgeons next morning removed seven pellets, but they had to leave the one in the neck as it was too risky to be taken out. They told me it's now part of your body. They've assured me that it would not cause any danger in future."More than 10 days later, Irshad says he's "still in some pain".A senior hospital official told the BBC that Irshad's injuries were caused by "pellet-type small particles", but would not say whether they were fired from a gun. "That's for the forensics to say once they've examined these pellets," they said.When the first claims of pellet gun use, external emerged last week, Delhi police, external called it "completely false and misleading". They said they did not even possess pellet guns. Since then, Indian media has reported that the shots were fired by the RAF, which reports to the paramilitary Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF). The BBC has reached out to CRPF chief Gyanendra Pratap Singh and also sent him questions on email. He's yet to respond.On Wednesday, government minister Jitendra Singh said in parliament that no "bullets" were fired, external and only tear gas was used. But he did not comment on the use of pellet guns.He was responding to allegations by Rahul Gandhi, Congress party MP and leader of the opposition in the lower house, who demanded that Home Minister Amit Shah be sacked since both the Delhi police and CRPF report to Shah.Last Saturday, Gandhi addressed a press conference accompanied by Sahil Lochab, a 19-year-old Delhi University student, who may lose an eye to pellet injuries. One side of Sahil's face and the back of his right arm are peppered with tiny holes. Gandhi lifted his T-shirt to reveal dozens more wounds on his underarm and body.In a video chat with Gandhi and in media interviews, Sahil said he supported the CJP protest, which centred around the issue of repeated paper leaks of key exams, because he wrote an exam to join the police force last year which was cancelled because of the same issue.He had gone to the protest with three friends but got separated in the chaos when police charged the crowd with batons. He was shot while marching towards the security forces with other protesters."I couldn't see who fired the pellet gun but it came from the side where the forces were," he said. "My right eye was swollen so much that it felt it had popped out of my face, I couldn't raise my right arm. I was bleeding profusely and some of the protesters took me to the hospital."His family, he told Gandhi, had tried to dissuade him from going to the protest, but "I couldn't stop myself"."I want justice. Whoever did this to me doesn't deserve to be in power," he said.Follow BBC News India on Instagram, external, YouTube,, external Twitter, external and Facebook, external.Clarification - 1 August: This story was updated to remove a reference to shotguns - or pellet guns - being widely used in the UK to shoot birds of prey, which is illegal.

schema.headline: CJP protest: India's 'Cockroach' protesters have wounds consistent with pellet-gun fire, experts say

title: Why limited war with the US may suit Iran better than peace
description: At first glance, Iran's surprise missile strike on a US base in Jordan earlier this week appeared difficult to explain. The attack effectively ended t
body: At first glance, Iran's surprise missile strike on a US base in Jordan earlier this week appeared difficult to explain. The attack effectively ended the fragile pause in direct US-Iran fighting and prompted Washington to resume strikes inside Iran. It was also unusual.If Tehran's priority had been a ceasefire, the strike is difficult to explain. But if Iranian leaders judge that a controlled confrontation could offer greater strategic leverage, the decision becomes more understandable.One possible explanation is that Tehran believes that, despite its risks, a limited war serves its interests better.Today, neither side appears ready for an all-out war. Washington has shown little appetite for a much broader regional conflict that could threaten energy infrastructure in the region, draw in more countries, push oil prices higher, and further stretch US military resources.Iran may also try to avoid an all-out war because its weakened air defences, vulnerable industrial infrastructure and sanctions-constrained economy make rebuilding losses increasingly difficult and expensive.Iran may have concluded that this creates room for a strategy based not on military victory but on sustained pressure.A prolonged ceasefire under current conditions could actually leave Tehran in a weaker position. The US naval blockade of Iranian ports would continue, sanctions would remain, and Iran would still be largely excluded from international energy markets.Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar and other oil and gas exporting countries in the region could gradually resume normal exports while Iran remained economically isolated.A limited conflict could change this landscape for Iran. Although Iran is paying a heavy military and economic price, disruption in the Strait of Hormuz and, through the Houthis, pressure around Bab al-Mandab continue to affect global shipping, insurance costs and energy markets. Even limited uncertainty forces governments, shipowners and importers to pay attention to Iran's demands.In effect, Tehran may believe it still possesses leverage.Iran also appears to be trying to reshape the diplomatic discussion. Rather than accepting unrestricted freedom of navigation, it has repeatedly signalled that shipping should operate under rules agreed with or administered by Iran. If that interpretation is correct, Tehran's objective may be that any future reopening of the Strait of Hormuz reflects Iranian influence rather than a return to the pre-war status quo. An ongoing, limited conflict would allow Iran to keep the pressure on to achieve this goal.From Tehran's perspective, keeping the crisis alive below the threshold of total war may therefore be preferable to accepting a ceasefire that leaves sanctions, the blockade and economic isolation largely unchanged.There may also be domestic calculations. Iran continues to face very high inflation rates, unemployment, economic hardship and public dissatisfaction. During periods of external conflict, governments often find it easier to suppress internal opposition, justify tighter security measures and rally support around national defence. That does not remove Iran's economic problems, but it may reduce the immediate political pressure created by them.None of this means the strategy is without significant costs. Iran continues to absorb repeated military strikes, economic uncertainty, and there is no guarantee that the current balance can be sustained.That is the main paradox facing Tehran. A controlled conflict may currently offer more leverage than an imperfect peace, but controlled conflicts have a habit of becoming uncontrolled. Iran may believe it can calibrate escalation carefully enough to keep pressure on the United States, global energy markets and regional diplomacy while avoiding all-out war.But that calculation also carries significant risks. Beyond the possibility of a much wider war, a prolonged conflict with no clear end in sight could gradually strengthen international support for a tougher response. There are already signs that the conflict is widening. Saudi Arabia, which had initially sought to avoid becoming directly involved, has carried out strikes against Iran-aligned Shia groups in Iraq and taken military action against the Houthis. If disruption to global trade and energy markets continues, other countries that have so far tried to remain on the sidelines could become more willing to support efforts to increase pressure on Iran.Some governments may also conclude that bearing the costs of a more robust response is preferable to living with repeated crises affecting international shipping and energy supplies.Whether those possibilities laid out above - including more countries getting actively involved - prove correct remains uncertain. Much may depend on whether Tehran is able to maintain calibrated actions without triggering a response that fundamentally changes the political and military calculations of the United States. The next unexpected strike could determine which path the conflict takes.

schema.headline: Why limited war with the US may suit Iran better than peace

title: Greyhounds bound for Australia as New Zealand racing ban takes effect
description: At least two chartered flights carrying up to 150 greyhounds are set to fly to Australia's eastern states, as a New Zealand ban on the sport comes int
body: At least two chartered flights carrying up to 150 greyhounds are set to fly to Australia's eastern states, as a New Zealand ban on the sport comes into effect.Several greyhound trainers in New Zealand are responding to a new ban by moving their dogs to Australia with plans to continue in the sport, governing body Greyhound Racing New Zealand (GRNZ) told the BBC.While the ban across New Zealand takes effect on Saturday, the practice remains legal almost everywhere in Australia.The ban was first announced in December 2024, and legislated in April. Approximately 1,400 greyhounds will retire in New Zealand under the ban and require rehoming.Australian authorities say that greyhounds arriving from New Zealand are classed as "companion animals" which will undergo screening for diseases such as rabies."Australia's import requirements for dogs are based on biosecurity risk, not the intended use of the animal," Australia's Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry told a Senate inquiry in June.A spokesperson for New Zealand's Racing Minister Winston Peters called the plans to relocate the dogs "the last gasp actions of a dying industry". Peters said the dog racing industry had "lost its social licence" after multiple reviews concluded that dog and injury death rates "remain unacceptably high", a conclusion that GRNZ disputed.In a statement, a spokesperson for Peters said: "We understand a small number of dogs are being exported to Australia, but the vast majority (1,300 to 1,400) will be rehomed over the next couple of years." "This is a one-off final act rather than an ongoing issue," the spokesperson added.GRNZ Edward Rennell chief executive told the BBC that between six and 10 trainers have expressed interest in relocating to Australia, with most New Zealand citizens not requiring a special visa to live in Australia. Details would be finalised "over the next two weeks", he said.Rennell said "the details aren't locked in" but that his organisation would cover the full cost of the flights, while other costs would be borne by owners and trainers."We will be supporting people that are looking to transfer over," Rennell said.He said some of the dogs will continue training and racing in Australia, although he noted they are likely to be less competitive in professional racing because breeding has largely paused in New Zealand since the ban was announced 18 months ago.Kiwis are still able to bet on Australian greyhound racing, which has a larger commercial presence.Queensland, New South Wales (NSW) and Victoria's industries were collectively worth almost A$2bn (£1.04bn; $1.4m) in 2022-23, which dwarfed New Zealand's $147m total, according to the latest figures published by Greyhounds Australasia.The dedicated body overseeing the closure of the industry in New Zealand, the Greyhound Transition Agency told the BBC: "We understand that arrangements are being made to relocate some dogs to Australia for racing purposes. "However, we are not in a position to comment further on these arrangements."New Zealand announced the greyhound racing ban following three independent reviews into the sport in 2013, 2017 and 2021."We acknowledge the industry made advances in safety, but the high injury and death rates persisted with no sign of improvement," Peters's spokesperson added.In response, Rennell told the BBC: "I will go to my grave saying that the greyhound welfare standards are the best of any racing code in New Zealand."GRNZ has eyed kennels across eastern Australia as destinations for New Zealand's racing dogs.A spokesperson for the Queensland Racing Integrity Commission said the agency "has been advised by Greyhound Racing New Zealand of the arrival of racing greyhounds and the potential relocation of industry participants from New Zealand into Queensland".NSW and Victorian officials said they were not aware of specific relocation plans within their states, noting that greyhounds are permitted to travel across jurisdictions in Australia in New Zealand.Australia's Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry did not respond to a request to make further comment.Dozens of greyhounds were also found to have been moved to Australia after New Zealand's ban was first announced.Officials have confirmed 80 greyhounds were exported from New Zealand to Queensland through a chartered flight in April 2025.One trainer and his family were drawn to the "shining lights of the new facility" west of Brisbane, Simon Stout from Greyhounds Australasia told a parliamentary committee hearing in Tasmania on Wednesday.But one federal senator, Mehreen Faruqi of the Greens, told the BBC she was "deeply concerned about loopholes that allow the continued export of racing dogs to this country that neither New Zealand nor Australia seem to care about". Director of the Coalition for the Protection of Greyhounds Kylie Field said Australia already struggles to find residential homes for thousands of retired racing dogs, including 4,100 in NSW."In an attempt to solve the rehoming crisis, the racing industry had devised a program of sending retired greyhounds to the US and Canada," Field said."More than 2,000 dogs have been sent overseas so far." Dog racing is banned in the Australian Capital Territory and Tasmania has announced plans to phase it out.Scotland and Wales both passed legislation outlawing commercial dog racing this year. Most US states have imposed a ban, leaving two racing tracks in West Virginia as the last active operations.

schema.headline: Greyhounds bound for Australia as New Zealand racing ban takes effect

title: Bowen: Plan for Hamas to disarm faces big obstacles, yet it offers rare hope for Gaza
description: There are many reasons why it might not work. At the same time, it is potentially a rare chink of light in a bleak picture. Hamas has never agreed to
body: There are many reasons why it might not work. At the same time, it is potentially a rare chink of light in a bleak picture. Hamas has never agreed to disarm before now. Handled carefully and well, there is a chance now to make diplomatic progress.A bargain lies at the heart of the new proposition for Hamas to disarm in Gaza.The idea is that as Hamas hands over its weapons, Israel pulls out of the 70% of Gaza that it occupies.That may sound simple, but the realities of politics, war, zero trust, the deaths of thousands and the destruction of Gaza make the process very complicated.Life in Gaza is catastrophic for well over 2 million Palestinian civilians who are living in desperate conditions. For most, Israel has destroyed their homes and their livelihoods. Israel killed more than 70,000 Palestinians during the war, and more than 1,000 more since the ceasefire, according to the Hamas-run health ministry whose figures are seen as reliable by the UN. Unicef says that Israel has killed more than 20,000 children since 7 October 2023, with at least 1,000 babies among the dead and wounded.Much of Gaza is rubble. It is not just the damage caused by Israel Defense Forces (IDF) military operations. There has also been an organised, officially sponsored project to destroy communities and smash infrastructure. Civilian demolition contractors from Israel have been contracted to finish the job started by IDF bombs.Many Palestinians believe Israel wants to force them out, by making life so insupportable and appalling that they will leave if they get the chance. Leaders and senior officials inside Jordan and Egypt also believe that powerful individuals in the Israeli government are working to create the conditions for the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians, most likely across their borders.On the Israeli side, there is a strong sense in the Jewish majority of 80% or so that Hamas will remain a potentially deadly threat until it is totally disarmed and stripped of any vestige of power. On 7 October 2023 Hamas and other Palestinians attacked Israel, killing almost 1,200 people, around two thirds of whom were civilians including children, and taking 251 people into Gaza as hostages.  Many Israelis believe Hamas would do that again if it had the chance.Follow live: Hamas agrees to Trump's plan to disarm in Gaza, official tells BBC, with Israel yet to commentHamas says it has agreed to disarm after Trump announces Board of Peace planThe diplomatic process that produced the agreement with Hamas does not operate in a bubble. Making the plan work depends on broader issues too.Israel has a general election at the end of October. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is behind in the polls and fighting not just for his political life and legacy but potentially for his liberty. While he remains in office, his long running trial on corruption charges that could carry a jail sentence has been slowed to a crawl. That would change if he lost power.Netanyahu faces pressure at home and abroad. Domestically he does not want his political opponents to be able to accuse him of being soft on Hamas. Internationally the only address that matters to him is in Washington DC.The US also has elections looming with midterms in November. President Donald Trump cannot achieve a win in the war on Iran, so he needs one in Gaza. If Trump's Republican party loses badly, the power he relishes using will drain away. Trump will blame Netanyahu if he decides he is preventing the victory he wants and needs.One of Netanyahu's boasts to Israel's electorate is that he can handle the Americans, including Trump, better than any of his rivals. A Trump tirade before election day in Israel scuppers that proposition.Netanyahu is an expert at playing for time when faced with a big challenge. He will try to juggle pressure at home and pressure from the Oval Office until election day.Hamas is also under severe pressure. Most of its senior men and thousands of its fighters were killed by Israel. The IDF still assassinates senior Hamas figures when it gets a chance. As I write, a flash from the IDF on my phone says it has killed a commander of a Palestinian militia who it says took hostages on 7 October 2023.Many Palestinians blame Hamas for the consequences of its decision to attack Israel on 7 October. Hamas also faces challenges from powerful families and by militias funded and backed by Israel.It is trying to rebuild grass roots support. This was how the BBC's Gaza correspondent Rushdi Abu Alouf put it to me: "For months, Hamas increasingly shifted part of its focus back to social and political outreach, expanding Quran memorisation programmes and charitable activities aimed at children, teenagers and young people, while taking advantage of the severe humanitarian crisis and the growing dependence of so many families on aid."Khalil al Hayya, the newly confirmed political leader of Hamas, was a crucial player in the decision to drop objections to the framework. Egypt and Turkey did much of the hard diplomatic work to get him there.Hamas concessions are linked to Israel agreeing to pull back in Gaza. Israel is on record as demanding full Hamas disarmament as a pre-condition for withdrawal.Only a step-by-step agreement, starting small and building confidence, has a chance of working. Trump will have to stay engaged, which is far from certain with a war with Iran among a planet full of other challenges.Just keeping the process going will require sustained diplomatic engagement and no sudden shocks that make meditation impossible.That will be difficult. The occupied West Bank is on the verge of an explosion of even worse violence. Figures gathered by ACLED, a group that monitors armed conflict, says that 2026 is on track to become the most violent year in the West Bank since it began monitoring the territory a decade ago.Jewish settlers have been allowed by the IDF and encouraged by extremists in the Netanyahu government to run riot, attacking and sometimes killing Palestinians and driving them off their land.Palestinians have been organising themselves to resist. Some opponents and critics of Netanyahu believe that he wants a major crisis on the West Bank to justify a tough response before the elections and remove any pressure to pull back in Gaza.Netanyahu and prominent ministers in his cabinet have said repeatedly that there will never be a Palestinian state. Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister, is committing the government to decisions aimed at increasing Jewish settlement and killing off the prospects of an independent Palestine. Smotrich is an extreme religious nationalist who has been sanctioned by major Western countries and banned from entering the UK, France, other leading European nations, as well as Australia and New Zealand. Israel condemned those decisions as antisemitic.A process that does not give Palestinians a political horizon and a route to self-determination will not work, condemning another generation to lives dominated by war.Diplomatic failure would not benefit Palestinians or Israelis. It would play into the hands of those on both sides who believe their conflict has no solution other than defeating their enemy.

schema.headline: Bowen: Plan for Hamas to disarm faces big obstacles, yet it offers rare hope for Gaza

title: Will Fifa president Gianni Infantino lose his job? If so, who comes in?
description: Infantino on the brink? Who might replace him if he goes?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Fifa president Gianni Infantino arrives for the Worl
body: Infantino on the brink? Who might replace him if he goes?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Fifa president Gianni Infantino arrives for the World Cup final on 19 JulyByChief football news reporterUpdated 1 August 2026 11:02 BSTLife moves fast for Fifa president Gianni Infantino.It was doing so last month as he was zig-zagging across the United States in a private jet to make him virtually omnipresent as the World Cup reached its crescendo.On 19 July he must have felt on top of the world as, together with US President Donald Trump, they handed the trophy over to Spain.Less than two weeks later, Infantino is in a lonely place after scrapping controversial plans to sell off stakes in Fifa competitions to private investment.Condemned by UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, castigated by fans of the game he professes to want to protect. These can easily be deflected as hazards of the job.Less so the threatened boycott of Fifa competitions by European governing body Uefa, and its subsequent stunning statement in which it declared it had lost confidence in Infantino's leadership.Concacaf (North and Central America and the Caribbean) and the AFC (Asia) also - in their own ways - have offered withering assessments of how Fifa is being run under Infantino."This issue extends far beyond a single proposal," said the AFC. "Rather, it has exposed fundamental weaknesses in Fifa's consultation and decision-making processes that must now be addressed."Sources say, in addition to rejecting Infantino's plan, the vast majority of the Concacaf members are either losing faith in the Fifa president's ability to govern the game, or have lost it altogether.On top of that, Carlos Cordeiro, special adviser to Infantino and appointed by Trump as senior adviser to the White House Task Force on the 2026 World Cup, has resigned.Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said in a statement to Associated Press that Fifa's own administration was "deceived" about the project.BBC Sport has approached Fifa for comment.It feels as though the walls are closing in on Infantino.But if this is the beginning of the end of his tenure, who takes over?Might Infantino really go?Firstly, it is wise to be realistic.Speaking to BBC Sport earlier this week, former Football Association chairman David Bernstein said of Infantino: "In a normal organisation, if he has to back down due to something of this magnitude he'd probably be shown the door."But Fifa is not a normal organisation. If he has the support of enough of the national associations, he will continue."Former Fifa vice-president Jim Boyce said he thought Infantino would "still have enough support" to be re-elected but "if things continue at the pace they are continuing, who knows?"He added: "If I was a betting man, which I'm not, I would still bet he will get his final four-year term."Infantino has been Fifa president since 2016. Before that he was secretary general of Uefa for seven years. Few know the map of football politics better than him.Now 56, Infantino became president by beating Asian Football Confederation president Sheikh Salman al-Khalifa by 115 votes to 88. His task was to clean up an organisation tainted by corruption allegations following the resignation of predecessor Sepp Blatter. Blatter was cleared of corruption charges last year."I will work tirelessly to bring football back to Fifa and Fifa back to football," said Infantino at the time.He has twice been re-elected unopposed, and it was expected the same thing would happen again next March. This is not unusual. Blatter was unopposed in 2007 and 2011.Brazilian Joao Havelange was the last person to unseat a Fifa president in an election, ousting Sir Stanley Rous in 1974. No-one opposed Havelange for five straight terms until he finally resigned in 1998, aged 82.Letters of support backing Infantino's re-election have been submitted. Will they be withdrawn?Who might replace him?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Concacaf president Victor Montagliani consoles Lionel Messi after Argentina's World Cup final defeat by SpainVictor Montagliani (Concacaf president)Like Infantino, he was elected in 2016 promising governance reform. A former president of Canada Soccer, Montagliani was heavily involved in the build up to, and delivery of the 2026 World Cup, the first to be hosted by three nations. He is fluent in French, Italian and Spanish, as well as English.Explaining his decision to run for the Concacaf presidency, Montagliani told the BC Business website: "Like anything, when I decide to go, I go. I campaigned on my own dime for three months, went to see all 41 countries, from the US to Bonaire, a little island off Venezuela."Montagliani took the lead when Concacaf hosted an expanded Copa America in 2024 - in an interview with BBC Sport he rejected the idea it could become a regular occurrence. Politically strong, he smoothed relations around Arsene Wenger's attempt to gain support for a World Cup every two years and has never truly bought into the idea of a 64-team World Cup.At the Leaders conference in 2025, he outlined why he felt football was strong enough to ride out any storm."The game is bigger than world current leaders," he said. "Football will survive regimes. Does it cause a headache? Of course. You have to be realistic about that. That is the beauty of our game, it is bigger than any individual and country."Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa (AFC president)Initially elected in 2013, he was elected unopposed for a fourth term to run to 2027.The Bahraini has presided over significant growth within the Asian confederation, through the Champions League Elite, Champions League Two, the Challenge League and the Women's Champions League, which was launched in 2024-25. The Asian Cup has been expanded to 24 teams.Sheikh Salman signed off the brutal takedown of how Fifa is being run by Infantino and has carried with him a 46-member confederation, many of whom are aware the figures being offered by Infantino's plan are huge in terms of their overall football expenditure.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, PSG president Nasser Al-Khelaifi (left) with manager Luis Enrique after the Champions League final victory over Arsenal in MayNasser Al-Khelaifi (PSG president and chair of European Football Clubs)Al-Khelaifi took over as chairman of the European Clubs' Association in the aftermath of the other seismic event that threatened to pull the game apart - the ill-fated European Super League, which collapsed within 48 hours in 2021.Al-Khelaifi presided over a name change - to European Football Clubs. More importantly, he expanded it to more than 800 members. Of the biggest clubs, only Real Madrid remain outside.In theory, the Qatari would be a serious challenger to Infantino. But it seems he doesn't want the role. "He genuinely, genuinely, genuinely doesn't want the job," was the response of a source close to the 52-year-old when asked about the possibility on Thursday.Mattias Grafstrom (Fifa secretary general)Appointed in May 2024 and an increasingly influential voice around the Fifa table.Multi-lingual Grafstrom become Infantino's chief of staff following his election as president in 2016.Another very visual presence at the World Cup, he could be seen as being too close to Infantino - and the general feeling Fifa's next president needs to be a non-European might also count against him.Fifa's next president will be confirmed at the organisation's 77th Congress in Morocco next March. Candidates have until 18 November to put their names forward.

schema.headline: Will Fifa president Gianni Infantino lose his job? If so, who comes in?

title: Nine killed in strikes on Kyiv, as Ukraine sinks Russian ship
description: At least nine people have been killed and dozens injured in Russian ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said
body: At least nine people have been killed and dozens injured in Russian ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said. Moscow has escalated deadly ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv recently, prompting Zelensky to say that missile interceptors are urgently needed.The strikes come two days after a suspected Russian cruise missile landed in Poland during a widespread attack on Ukraine that killed at least eight people, including six members of one family.Separately, Ukrainian drones sank a Russian-owned container ship in the Black Sea on Saturday. Moscow said all 17 crew were rescued. Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the capital had come under a ballistic missile attack on Saturday, with AFP reporting more than 10 explosions. Fires broke out across the city and power cuts were reported in some areas.Klitschko said a residential building in Shevchenkivskyi was partially destroyed, trapping people inside. The emergency services said at least seven people were killed in a strike in the Darnytskyi district. Another 14 were injured, including two children, it reported.In Solomyanskyi district, two people died and eight were injured, including two children, as a five-storey residential building was partially destroyed, officials said.A missile landed near the Lithuanian embassy, breaking windows and scattering debris in the compound, Lithuania's foreign ministry said.Zelensky said in a post on X that the sanctioned 100,000-tonne capacity container ship Yanina had been "sent to the bottom". Moscow confirmed the attack in a statement from state-owned nuclear operator Rosatom, which owns the ship. Rosatom said it had been transporting civilian goods including frozen food and construction materials, adding that the attack took place 130 miles (209km) from Novorossiysk."Such an attack cannot be interpreted as anything other than piracy and robbery," Rosatom's CEO Alexey Likhachev said, adding that all 17 crew members were in a "satisfactory" condition.Ukraine has targeted Russian-flagged ships in the Black Sea since Russia's full-scale invasion of the country in 2022. The attack on Kyiv comes after Zelensky met President Donald Trump in Washington DC earlier this week to urge the US to grant Ukraine a licence to produce Patriot interceptor missiles.Asked about the missiles during a cabinet meeting at the Camp David retreat on Friday, Trump said the US had not agreed to Ukraine building Patriot missiles but that talks were ongoing.He said the US had to be "very careful about letting somebody build them".Emphasising concerns about sharing advanced US weaponry, Trump called it "a big step".Trump's latest comments regarding Patriot missiles come weeks after he offered to give Ukraine the right to produce them.As Russia has stepped up its air attacks, Ukraine has run low on supplies of Patriots, which remain the only weapon in its arsenal capable of downing ballistic missiles.

schema.headline: Nine killed in strikes on Kyiv, as Ukraine sinks Russian ship

title: What's in the Gaza peace deal roadmap?
description: ByYolande KnellMiddle East correspondentReporting fromJerusalemHamas says it has accepted a disarmament plan for Gaza which will see it lay down its a
body: ByYolande KnellMiddle East correspondentReporting fromJerusalemHamas says it has accepted a disarmament plan for Gaza which will see it lay down its arms - a decision US President Donald Trump has described as "a monumental step toward lasting peace and security".The group said it had negotiated "responsibly and positively" and reached "national consensus" among the Palestinian factions. Israel – which remains highly sceptical about Hamas's willingness to disarm  –  says it will not withdraw from Gaza until it does so. In addition to a 15-point roadmap published by the US-led Board of Peace, the BBC has seen a four-page plan for the phased disarmament of Hamas and gradual Israeli withdrawal.What does the plan say about Hamas disarming?Hamas giving up its weapons - as predicted - has been a main sticking point in advancing President Trump's 20-point plan for ending the war in Gaza.That plan, unveiled in September last year, included the creation of the Board of Peace to oversee the agreement's implementation and "handle the funding for the redevelopment of Gaza".The principles in the roadmap and the document seen by the BBC say: "A process shall begin to inventory and store heavy weapons, military production sites, weapons depots, and tunnels".  It says this is conditional on Israel meeting its commitments under the initial ceasefire agreement reached in October last year.This clause still sounds like a significant breakthrough. The process would be overseen by the Palestinian National Committee - a group of independent technocrats to which Hamas has agreed to hand over power - and with the deployment of the International Stabilisation Force to Gaza.  The document refers not just to Hamas but other Palestinian factions joining the disarmament process.The roadmap documents then links this "to a phased Israeli withdrawal" and specifies that "no weapons shall be transferred or handed over to Israel or to any non-Palestinian party".Can this be done?The exact mechanism of how the handover of weapons would work is not clear. It is believed that all heavy weapons – including Hamas's remaining rockets - and other military hardware would be moved into a secure storage managed by the National Committee. As yet, the committee has not entered Gaza. It has been working from Cairo.In terms of timeframe, the document we have seen says only that this would happen "in a gradual, sequential, and time-bound manner, based on an implementation schedule to be prepared within 14 days."Hamas has since said giving up its heavy weapons is contingent on Israel ending "all forms of aggression" and withdrawing its forces from Gaza.Israel's commitment to ending its attack on Gaza is a "fundamental prerequisite" for moving forward with the deal, the group said in a statement.Underground tunnel networks, weapons stores and manufacturing sites would be mapped and destroyed.Remaining personal arms and police weapons would need to be registered and handed over in stages to the new Palestinian police force working under the supervision of the International Stabilisation Force (ISF).  Hundreds of new Palestinian police recruits have already been trained in Egypt and Jordan.  Israel's cabinet recently approved some 200 international troops from "friendly countries" entering Gaza as part of the ISF, but it has not yet been deployed.Hamas has been seeking assurances that pro-Israel militia in Gaza will be dismantled and will also give up their arms.What does Israel make of the plan?Israel is deeply sceptical about Hamas' willingness to give up its weapons or its control in Gaza.  Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir said via Telegram, external the plan is "not acceptable" to Israel. Israeli officials have insisted that there will be no Israeli withdrawal from the Yellow Line - which demarcates the area it controls - before Hamas is disarmed.What makes this more unclear is that Israel currently controls more than the 53% of Gaza in which its troops were set to remain under the terms of the October ceasefire deal. As the BBC has recently reported, yellow concrete blocks delineating the Yellow Line have been moved westwards so that Israel controls more than 60% of the strip.Part of the document seen by the BBC is an annex. This requires Israeli forces to withdraw to the agreed Yellow Line "within 24 hours of the Israeli government's approval of the plan." It says they should not return "as long as Hamas complies with the implementation of the agreement."The plan talks about civil servants – what is this about?Hamas announced earlier this month that it had dissolved its government in Gaza and was preparing to transfer power to the National Committee as part of the ceasefire deal. In negotiations it has wanted to ensure that the tens of thousands of civil servants that its government employed in Gaza prior to the war should be compensated or given new jobs.The public workers include Hamas police and security forces but also health and education staff. Many, though not all, are likely to be supporters of Hamas.The plan agrees to treat all public employees "lawfully, fairly, and with dignity regarding their rights."  It remains to be seen what security vetting will be used for civil servants working with the National Committee.Why is Hamas agreeing now?In recent talks on advancing Trump's peace plan, Hamas has been put under intense pressure from regional mediators - who were themselves being pushed by Washington to show progress.The recent appointment of the Hamas chief negotiator, Khalil al-Hayya as overall leader of the group - replacing a five-member council - has simplified decision-making.  He has strong backing from Gaza members and the Hamas armed wing.Regional events may also have played a role in timing. Early in the Iran war, Hamas officials were said to be taking more hardline positions, hoping that Tehran - a backer of the group - would emerge victorious and that this would strengthen their position. Those close to Hamas, say they have since lost hope in this idea.Palestinian officials involved in the talks suggest the new leadership was ready to take this landmark political decision driven by the devastating humanitarian conditions in Gaza.What is it like in Gaza today?The announcement has, so far, been met with little enthusiasm in Gaza, though some people told the BBC they saw a glimmer of hope. After years of failed ceasefires and collapsed agreements, many Palestinians have grown deeply sceptical of a new political deal.The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) confirmed to the BBC earlier reports of an Israeli strike on Gaza just hours after Trump announced the deal, in which it was reported that several Palestinians were injured.More than two million Palestinians are living in terrible conditions in Gaza, battling disease, a lack of access to food, clean water, and adequate shelter.These people are living in a shrinking chunk of land, as Israel continues to build land barriers, further displacing families and expanding its "Yellow Line" temporary control area deeper into the territory.At least 1,168 Palestinians including children have been killed in Israeli attacks since the ceasefire took effect, according to figures from the Hamas health ministry whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.Four Israeli soldiers have been killed in Palestinian attacks in Gaza over the same period.Israel has destroyed more than 1,500 buildings in areas of Gaza that have remained under its control since the ceasefire, satellite images seen by BBC Verify last November showed. The actual number is likely much higher, with imagery unavailable for some areas.According to UN estimates, around 60 million tonnes of debris has been generated since October 2023.

schema.headline: What's in the Gaza peace deal roadmap?

title: Trump administration drops Reflecting Pool vandalism charge and admits 'botched' repairs
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByMax Matza and Kwasi Gyamfi AsieduUpdated 3 hours agoUS prosecutors have dropped charges against a former Olympian who had
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByMax Matza and Kwasi Gyamfi AsieduUpdated 3 hours agoUS prosecutors have dropped charges against a former Olympian who had been accused of vandalising the Reflecting Pool in Washington DC, saying the damage is now believed to be "the result of flawed installation by the contractor".A court document filed on Friday said new information "strongly suggests that a rushed and botched installation" job overseen by the US Department of the Interior led to the damage.On Saturday, President Donald Trump conceded "there may have been some contractor difficultly" but reiterated his claim that the "major damage" was caused by vandals.David Hearn, a champion canoeist, had been facing a 10-year prison sentence if found guilty after his arrest last month.Image source, The Washington Post via Getty ImagesImage caption, A piece of the new blue paint could be seen peeling off the bottom of the pool on ThursdayIn a statement, Hearn's lawyers accused the Trump administration of abuse of power, and said it "owes Mr Hearn an apology".Hearn previously told the BBC that he "didn't destroy, rip, tear, peel, or remove any part" of the paint in the pool. Asked by the BBC on Friday if he is planning legal action over the government missteps that led to the charges and false public accusations, he declined to comment.The document filed by US Attorney for Washington DC Jeanine Pirro blames contractors for rushing the paint installation process as part of Trump's efforts to beautify the city ahead of the country's 250th independence anniversary on 4 July.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The pool was drained again in JulyHearn was arrested after he said he reached down to touch the pool after a bike ride in the area. He was not the only one. At least three others were charged with vandalism, court records show. Five more received citations from police, an administration official told CBS News, the BBC's US partner. They include one person who Trump claimed had used a blade to "put a 250 foot long gash into the beautiful facade". It's unclear if all of the charges now have been dropped.In the court filing on Friday, the Trump administration said new information from the Department of Interior (DOI) indicated "that damage to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in June 2026 was the result of flawed installation by the contractor" and "the rush to complete the project prior to events associated with the America 250 celebration in the weeks surrounding Independence Day 2026"."It was not until after these documents were produced that [prosecutors] first became aware of information showing that the damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism as initially represented by DOI."Image source, ReutersImage caption, Former U.S. Olympic canoeist David HearnThe BBC has contacted the contractor for comment.Hearn's lawyers said in a statement to BBC News, that the case "should have never been brought"."Its dismissal today does not erase the abuse of government power in arresting and charging a patriotic American who did nothing wrong. The government's approach was ready, fire, aim."The Reflecting Pool underwent a multi-million dollar resealing and painting project this spring.The monument had long been beset by structural failures and leaks, and Trump championed the project as part of his bid to beautify the capital city.But, despite the makeover, which cost an estimated $16m (£12m), the pool had continued to be plagued by algae, and pieces of the blue sealant peeled off within days after its application.The project, whose original budget was less than $2m, was awarded to a contractor chosen by Trump himself, CBS reported, and was not open to bidding from other companies as is typical for government work. The admission on Friday represents a stunning about-face by Trump and his administration. Figure caption, How Washington DC's Reflecting Pool became a global talking pointThe US president at one point claimed the pool had been targeted by "sick, deranged" vandals, and was "given a 300 foot long gash" by a blade. Pirro accused Hearn of "a deliberate act to damage the Reflecting Pool."Pirro submitted the court filing on Friday dropping the vandalism claim and blaming the contractor for the botched job and Department of Interior officials for failing to provide prosecutors with complete information about what caused the problems with the pool."DOI provided less than fulsome information at the outset of this case," the document said. "Had DOI been forthcoming with the information clearly in its possession, the government would not have sought a grand jury indictment."On Saturday, Trump wrote on Truth Social that he disagreed "100%" with Pirro's decision to drop the charges, restating his claims about vandalism but admitting that other factors were in play."There may have been some contractor difficulty, but the major damage was caused by VANDALS!" the president wrote.Crews have now drained the Reflecting Pool for the second time in three months. It remains empty.Figure caption, Why has the renovated Reflecting Pool turned green?

title: Chelsea was murdered 10 years ago - will a new police podcast catch her killer?
description: Peter Chadwick had been on the run for nearly four years, charged with murdering his wife, when California police launched a podcast about the crime.H
body: Peter Chadwick had been on the run for nearly four years, charged with murdering his wife, when California police launched a podcast about the crime.He was captured in Mexico 10 months and 20 days later.Karen Schepers had been missing for more than four decades when another police force, in Illinois, debuted the first episode of a podcast last year about the cold case - and her body was found at the bottom of a river within weeks.Now Colorado investigators are hoping to bring in elusive tips about a 10-year-old unsolved murder, too. The Aurora Police Department (APD) released its own podcast this summer in an attempt to achieve justice for Chelsea Yasser, 21, who was found fatally stabbed in a shopping centre parking lot in 2016.As the barrelling behemoth of true crime content continues to flourish, police departments across the US and abroad are turning to podcast production for help solving cold murder cases and other investigations.Most departments don't have the staff, budget or time needed to produce podcast content, nor do they have the equipment or expertise.Others hold off for fear of repercussions, lawsuits and civil liability, says retired detective Alcazar.In California, Newport Beach Police Department's podcast about the fugitive Chadwick, for example, was not without controversy. The millionaire was introduced to viewers in Episode 1 as "a man who killed his wife in the peaceful coastal community of Newport Beach, California in October 2012".Chadwick had been charged and pleaded not guilty, but not tried - yet the podcast made no use of the word "alleged" and called the millionaire a "murderer". Critics argued that it flew in the face of innocent-before-proven-guilty parameters and that the job of police was to investigate, not adjudicate.The podcast was produced and hosted by public information officer Jennifer Manzella, who defended the choice at the time, saying police "put out the same kinds of statements all the time".She tells BBC News that she was trying to balance telling the story in an engaging way without jeopardising the investigation.After Chadwick's August 2019 apprehension, he pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and was sentenced to 15 years to life in prison - where he remains.Houghton and Vartarian had just been assigned to Elgin's new cold case unit in 2024 when the chief informed them that the job would also involve podcasting."We're already starting this new unit," Houghton recalls. "Why are we adding something else new on top of that?"Houghton and his partner begrudgingly began figuring out how to arrange episodes and soon discovered the process was also helping them structure the investigation. They formed different theories about what had happened to the missing 23-year-old, and each theory naturally formed an episode.The podcast not only generated tips but also gave the detectives more ways to find leads. They started going through posts on social media about their own programme."They'd say, like, 'Oh, my mom worked with this person, or I live in this neighbourhood and I remember this.'"The detectives ultimately solved the case through old-fashioned policework; one of their theories had been that Schepers had crashed her car and ended up in the river.They had found a 1999 local newspaper story claiming that police had searched salvage yards by helicopter as well as dragging the Fox River but there was no evidence the latter had happened.  And they did not shy away from telling listeners this.So the department brought in a search company with the latest sonar technology as well as divers - and they found Schepers and her car at the bottom of the river in March 2025.Now they're on the third season of the podcast. They shook up the format for the second, focusing on homicides, but have returned to a missing persons case.Houghton acknowledges that "it is a lot of work - it takes a lot of time and effort".As other departments navigate those budgetary and resource issues, however, there's a consensus that podcasts as an investigative tool will be seen more frequently.If police departments can find the staffing to sustain it, podcasting could help in both recruitment and staff retention, says Janice Iwama, associate professor in American University's department of justice, law and criminology. It gives listeners the chance to learn more about what policing is really like, from the mouths of working officers.Generational change could also fuel the trend, says retired NYPD Detective Alcazar, because younger police officers will be more ready to embrace the opportunities presented by podcasts and social media."That's their world," he says. "That's what they're most comfortable with."
